title: Saint Andrew Dũng-Lạc, Priest, and Companions, Martyrs
short_summary: Andrew Dũng-Lạc and his companions represent 117 martyrs killed in Vietnam between 1745 and 1862. The group includes Vietnamese laypeople and clergy as well as Dominican and other missionaries from Spain and France, drawn from several periods of persecution.
key_facts: Their memorial is celebrated on November 24.
The group contains 117 canonized martyrs: bishops, priests, religious, catechists, soldiers, parents, and other lay Catholics.
Ninety-six were Vietnamese and twenty-one were Spanish or French missionaries.
Pope John Paul II canonized the group together in Rome in 1988.

sections.heading: Christianity and persecution in Vietnam
sections.body: Christian missionaries reached Vietnam in the sixteenth century, and Catholic communities grew through the work of local catechists, families, clergy, and foreign religious orders. Different rulers alternated periods of tolerance with severe restrictions. Persecutions were driven by changing combinations of political suspicion, resistance to foreign influence, religious policy, and demands that Christians publicly renounce their faith.

sections.heading: Andrew Dũng-Lạc
sections.body: Born around 1795 to a poor non-Christian family in northern Vietnam, he was taken in and educated by a catechist, baptized with the name Andrew, and ordained a priest in 1823. He became known for preaching, a simple life, and assistance to the poor. After an arrest in 1835, parishioners paid for his release. He changed his surname from Dũng to Lạc, but was arrested again in 1839 with the priest Peter Trương Văn Thi. Both were beheaded at Hanoi on December 21.

sections.heading: A diverse company of martyrs
sections.body: The 117 saints died under several Vietnamese rulers and by different forms of execution. They include eleven Spanish Dominicans, ten members of the Paris Foreign Missions Society, and ninety-six Vietnamese Catholics. Among the Vietnamese were thirty-seven priests and fifty-nine laypeople. Their stories show that the Church in Vietnam was not simply a foreign mission but a community rooted in local families and leaders.

sections.heading: Canonization and memory
sections.body: The martyrs had been beatified in separate groups between 1900 and 1951. John Paul II canonized them together on June 19, 1988, giving the universal Church a single liturgical memorial. They stand for many other Vietnamese Christians whose names and circumstances were not preserved.

catholic_connection_sections.heading: A Church with local roots
catholic_connection_sections.body: The martyrs include more laypeople than foreign missionaries. Their witness belongs to Vietnamese Catholic history and shows how the faith was taught, sustained, and handed on by local communities.

catholic_connection_sections.heading: Freedom and fidelity
catholic_connection_sections.body: Many were offered life if they would trample a crucifix or deny Christ. Their memorial honors freedom of conscience and the conviction that political pressure cannot command a person's worship.

historical_cautions: Large estimates for the total number killed during Vietnamese persecutions vary and should be presented as estimates, not exact totals.
The 117 martyrs died across more than a century; avoid describing them as victims of a single event or ruler.
